name: Brepocitinib

lead: Brepocitinib is an oral, once-daily drug that blocks two enzymes in the JAK family, TYK2 and JAK1, which relay inflammatory cytokine signals including interferons, IL-12 and IL-23.[2] It was developed for autoimmune disease and has been tested in dermatomyositis, psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, hidradenitis suppurativa and hair-loss conditions.

For looks, the relevant use is autoimmune hair loss. A phase 2a trial tested it alongside ritlecitinib in alopecia areata, and a separate phase 2a trial tested it in scarring (cicatricial) alopecias such as lichen planopilaris.[8][7] Its main approval is for adult dermatomyositis, a condition with skin rash and muscle weakness; Wikipedia reports a US approval in August 2026.[11]

paras: It is a prescription medicine taken by mouth under specialist care, and in trials is compared with placebo over periods of 24 to 52 weeks. It is not a cosmetic product and is not used for ordinary pattern hair loss. Online discussion is limited and centers on interest in JAK inhibitors for alopecia areata generally.

Reported adverse reactions include upper respiratory infection, headache, fatigue, urinary tract infection and nausea.[11] Reviews of JAK-pathway drugs describe class concerns about infections, venous thromboembolism and malignancy, which TYK2-selective agents may partly differ on.[4][3] It is Rx-only and requires medical monitoring.

chain: Reduces immune attack on hair follicles
Hair may regrow in alopecia areata or slow scarring in cicatricial alopecia
angle.text: For people whose hair loss is autoimmune, brepocitinib was studied as a way to quiet the inflammation damaging follicles. It is not aimed at common androgenetic hair loss.

lead: Brepocitinib (code name PF-06700841) is an oral TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor.[1][2] By blocking these kinases it reduces signaling by type I and II interferons, IL-12 and IL-23, pathways implicated in several autoimmune and inflammatory skin and hair diseases.[1][2]

In autoimmune hair loss, immune cells attack the hair follicle; the aim of treatment is to calm that attack so hair can regrow. Brepocitinib was tested for alopecia areata in a phase 2a randomized, placebo-controlled study with ritlecitinib,[3] and for cicatricial alopecias including lichen planopilaris in a 52-week phase 2a trial.[4]

Its first marketed indication is dermatomyositis in adults. A phase 3 trial of 241 patients reported superiority of the 30 mg dose over placebo on the Total Improvement Score.[5] Wikipedia reports FDA approval in August 2026 under the brand Lisraya.[6]

paras: The phase 3 VALOR trial in dermatomyositis compared brepocitinib 30 mg, 15 mg and placebo for 52 weeks in 241 adults; the mean Total Improvement Score at week 52 was 46.5, 37.5 and 31.2 respectively.[5] Wikipedia lists dermatomyositis as the approved indication.[6]

Phase 2a trials examined alopecia areata[3] and cicatricial alopecia,[4] and earlier trials examined plaque psoriasis,[7] psoriatic arthritis[8] and hidradenitis suppurativa.[9] Psoriasis reviews note brepocitinib among JAK-pathway agents under investigation.[10][11]

TYK2 participates in signaling downstream of type I interferons, IL-12, IL-23 and IL-10, and a review notes it has a distinct set of immune effects from JAK1, JAK2 and JAK3.[2] Brepocitinib inhibits TYK2 and JAK1, reducing signaling by IFN-alpha/beta, IL-12, IL-23 and IFN-gamma.[1] Some reviewers suggest TYK2 inhibitors may have a safety profile that differs from broader JAK inhibitors.[2]

Common adverse reactions reported for the approved use include upper respiratory tract infection, headache, fatigue, urinary tract infection and nausea.[6] Reviews of JAK inhibitors in immune-mediated disease have raised class concerns about infections, venous thromboembolism and malignancy.[11]

A phase 2a randomized, placebo-controlled study evaluated oral ritlecitinib and brepocitinib in alopecia areata with 24-week results.[3] A 52-week phase 2a randomized trial examined brepocitinib in cicatricial alopecias, including lichen planopilaris.[4] Other phase 2 trials covered plaque psoriasis,[7] psoriatic arthritis[8] and hidradenitis suppurativa,[9] and the NEJM phase 3 trial covered dermatomyositis.[5] Detailed hair outcomes are in the trial publications.

Brepocitinib was developed first within Pfizer under the code PF-06700841 and later by Priovant Therapeutics, a Roivant company, according to Wikipedia's account of the approval.[6] It received orphan drug and priority review designations.[6] It is prescription-only.
